content: The guideline development process involved contributions from four WHO staff members from the Preventing Unsafe Abortion (PUA) Unit within the Department of Sexual and Reproductive Health and Research. Participants included young individuals (up to age 30) with proven leadership skills in adolescent sexual and reproductive health and rights, representing 13 countries across WHO regions. Discussions during the meeting focused on three main themes: youth values and preferences regarding abortion services, addressing barriers and abortion stigma, and scaling up promising practices and interventions. Key issues discussed included the components of an enabling environment and meaningful youth engagement. Members of the International Youth Alliance for Family Planning (IYAFP) are preparing a position paper as the primary output of the meeting. For further details, refer to Web Annex B: Technical meetings during guideline development. The Evidence and Recommendations Review Group (ERRG) held online meetings between March 2020 and March 2021, with 4–5 meetings for each of the three domains. Each meeting spanned two days and was facilitated by WHO technical officers and members of the WHO Steering Group. During these meetings, members of the Evidence Synthesis Teams presented systematic reviews of evidence. ERRG members reviewed and discussed the evidence, formulating draft recommendations, implementation considerations, and good practice statements for further review, revision, and finalization by the Guideline Development Group (GDG). Meetings were held for the following domains: Clinical services: March 2020, May 2020, June 2020, September 2020, February 2021. Service delivery: Pre-ERRG June 2020, October 2020, January 2021, early March 2021, late March 2021. Law and policy: March–April 2020, June 2020, August–September 2020, March 2021. The GDG meeting, held online from April 27–30, 2021, involved reviewing, discussing, revising, and finalizing draft recommendations, implementation considerations, and good practice statements across all three domains. The guideline considered various categories of health workers, with descriptions adapted to be generic enough for application across different settings. These descriptions are indicative and illustrative, not intended to replace formal definitions of professional bodies or titles used in specific countries. Categories included: Lay health workers, village health workers, female community health volunteers, trained birth attendants, trained helpline workers, abortion accompaniers, hotline counselors. Pharmacy workers, including technicians and assistants who dispense medicinal products under the guidance of a pharmacist. They may also prepare, store, and dispense medications and provide instructions on their use as prescribed by health professionals. Pharmacists, who are healthcare practitioners authorized to dispense medicinal products and counsel on their proper use and potential adverse effects. Traditional and complementary medicine professionals, trained in non-allopathic systems of medicine, often with a fouror five-year university degree. Auxiliary nurse midwives (ANMs) and auxiliary nurses, trained in basic nursing skills and some midwifery competencies but not fully qualified as midwives. Nurses, legally authorized to practice after examination by a regulatory authority. Midwives, trained in essential midwifery competencies, typically through three or more years of education leading to a university degree or equivalent. Advanced associate clinicians and associate clinicians, trained to diagnose and manage common medical and surgical conditions and perform some types of surgery. Monitoring and evaluation of quality abortion care involved identifying indicators through a scoping review and expert consultations conducted by scientists from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) and WHO. The scoping review summarized abortion measures and indicators reported between 2008 and 2018, screening 1,999 abstracts and seven additional documents, yielding 792 indicators from 142 documents. Findings were published in BMJ Global Health, with the indicators available in a searchable spreadsheet. An initial virtual consultation meeting in June 2020 presented multiple sets of indicators for global and program-level monitoring, including a subset of 17 core indicators selected from the scoping review and other initiatives. A total of 52 unique indicators were proposed during the consultation meeting. The WHO health systems strengthening monitoring and evaluation framework was presented as a potential structure for quality abortion monitoring and evaluation (M&E). During a consolidation phase, LSHTM and WHO scientists reduced the 52 indicators to 29, removing duplicates and ensuring relevance and feasibility for M&E. Six indicators were added to represent previously unaddressed categories in the health systems strengthening framework, aligning with Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) targets related to sexual and reproductive health and rights. An online consultation in March 2021 invited experts in abortion care measurement and M&E to review the 29 consolidated indicators. Twenty-two experts reviewed the indicators, categorized into areas such as governance, financing, infrastructure, information systems, health workforce, intervention access and readiness, intervention quality and safety, coverage, risk behaviors, health outcomes, responsiveness, and social protection. The core team from LSHTM and WHO is finalizing the indicator list, recognizing the need for periodic assessment to maintain utility and relevance. A report will be published in due course.
